title: Pasqal Nearly Doubled in Its Nasdaq Debut. A Real Quantum Company Just Got Priced Like a Promise.
subtitle: The French neutral-atom pioneer — seven deployed QPUs, a 200-qubit machine at Saudi Aramco, a Nobel laureate as chair — began trading Friday after closing its SPAC merger with Bleichroeder Acquisition Corp. II, and shares nearly doubled on day one. Now comes the hard part: living up to a valuation roughly 100 times revenue.
summary: Pasqal, the French quantum computing company that builds machines out of lasers and neutral atoms, began trading on Nasdaq Friday after completing its SPAC merger with Bleichroeder Acquisition Corp. II — and shares nearly doubled on debut. The company has real deployments: seven QPUs, systems at four national HPC centers, and a 200-qubit machine at Saudi Aramco. But with roughly $19 million in revenue and a valuation around 100 times sales, the first-day pop is only half the story.

bodyHtml:
Here's the thing about Friday's biggest tech debut: it wasn't a chatbot company or a cloud darling. It was a French outfit that builds quantum computers out of lasers and individual atoms — and its shares nearly doubled on day one. So what does Pasqal actually do, in one sentence you can repeat at dinner? It traps arrays of neutral atoms in precisely aimed laser light — 'optical tweezers' — then nudges them with more lasers to run calculations ordinary computers can't. No deep cryogenics, unlike the superconducting chips from IBM and Rigetti, or the trapped-ion machines from IonQ and Quantinuum. Lasers, atoms, physics: that's the whole machine.

Pasqal spun out of France's Institut d'Optique and CNRS in 2019, and its founding brain trust includes Alain Aspect — the 2022 Nobel laureate — who now chairs the company. It has about 275 employees, a CEO recruited from Amazon and Google, and something most quantum startups still can't claim: machines in the field, doing real work. Seven QPUs deployed, three in production, 25-plus commercial and research applications. Systems running at four national HPC centers — France's GENCI, Germany's Jülich, Italy's CINECA, and a Canadian site. Manufacturing in Palaiseau and Canada with capacity for roughly 13 systems a year. In May, Pasqal switched on a 200-qubit machine at Saudi Aramco's data center in Dhahran — Saudi Arabia's first quantum computer and the Middle East's first commercial quantum-computing-as-a-service. In June, CINECA took delivery of Italy's first neutral-atom system. Friday's listing took the scenic route. Pasqal agreed to merge with Bleichroeder Acquisition Corp. II in March at a $2 billion pre-money valuation, with a $200 million committed convertible financing attached. The deal closed this week with about $360 million in cash — SPAC redemptions trimmed the original haul. Then the stock did something SPAC stocks almost never do: it went up, and up hard. Which brings us to the uncomfortable question. Pasqal's last fiscal year brought in roughly $19 million in revenue, about double the year before. The market now values the company at roughly 100 times that — the prospectus itself spelled out a range around 95 to 100 times. It's math that makes value investors wince and momentum traders shrug, and there's no analyst coverage yet to referee the debate. Here's why this matters beyond the ticker. Quantum-AI convergence is now a listed-equities story, and Pasqal sits in the middle of it. Its machines plug into Nvidia's CUDA-Q stack and NVQLink — hybrid quantum-classical systems wired into the AI ecosystem — and it reaches customers through Google Cloud, Azure, and IBM's Quantum Network. Crédit Agricole, LG Electronics, EDF: the client list reads like a map of European industrial AI, and a new Pasqal Arabia joint venture with Aramco was announced just days before the listing. It's also a geopolitical story wearing a stock ticker. Washington is pumping $2 billion into quantum developers. Riyadh bought its first quantum computer from a French firm. Brussels funds EuroHPC quantum hosts, and Paris keeps a veto over non-European stakes in its quantum champions. The next compute layer is strategic infrastructure now, and governments are placing their bets. Pasqal lands in the middle of a 2026 quantum IPO wave — Infleqtion hit the NYSE earlier this summer — with the industry's Q-Day clock ticking in the background: the day quantum machines crack today's encryption. Neutral-atom systems are a serious contender in that race, which is exactly why Aramco, Jülich, and CINECA all picked this flavor. The roadmap: a 250-qubit machine on the way, and 10,000 physical qubits by 2030. There's about $80 million in booked and awarded business — grants and multi-year contracts — to fund the climb. The bull case is real machines, real customers, and a front-row seat in the quantum-AI race. The bear case is the price tag. Friday's pop settled that argument for exactly one day; the next few quarters of deliveries and contracts will settle the rest.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in PSQL. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
